records.name: Pennsylvania
records.current_summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Pennsylvania in its 'low-risk states' group — largely refraining from targeting transgender adults while not specialising in protection.

A national equality tracker records no public-facility-use ban for Pennsylvania, leaving the state's profile for a trans visitor defined by that restraint rather than by any affirmative statute in either direction.

sources.claim: Erin Reed's anti-trans legal-risk map (July 2026 update): places Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier — states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without specialising in protection — while documenting continued national degradation of trans rights through the 2026 legislative season.

sources.title: Pa. senators passed a transgender female athlete ban. Will the House take it up?
sources.claim: Pennsylvania's Senate on April 22, 2026 passed Senate Bill 1293, the 'Save Women's Sports Act', which would ban transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth; the Pennsylvania Capital-Star reports Gov. Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers 'extremists', and it was unclear whether the House would take the bill up. The measure targets youth school sports rather than transgender adults or public-facility access. The Senate's action and the governor's opposition frame the state's legal trajectory for a trans visitor.

sources.title: Pennsylvania Governor Vetoes Transgender Sports Ban
sources.claim: Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Wolf on July 11, 2022 vetoed legislation that would have barred transgender athletes from teams matching their gender identity by requiring public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with athletes in female-designated sports required to have been assigned female at birth. The bill had passed the Republican-led legislature on largely party-line votes. The veto documents Pennsylvania declining to enact an anti-trans measure, matching the record's low-risk grading.

sources.title: Senate Approves 'Save Women's Sports Act' to Protect Fairness in Female Athletics
sources.claim: The Pennsylvania Senate on May 6, 2025 approved Senate Bill 9, the 'Save Women's Sports Act', reserving athletic teams designated for women for 'biological females' in Pennsylvania's K-12 and collegiate sports and sending the bill to the House of Representatives. The press release from the Pennsylvania Senate Republican Caucus, with sponsors including Sens. Judy Ward and Kristin Phillips-Hill, confirms the state Senate has repeatedly backed trans-athlete restrictions for school sports. The measure concerns youth sports participation rather than adult care or public facilities.

records.name: Wisconsin
records.current_summary:
An independent July 2026 assessment of anti-trans legal risk across the United States classifies Wisconsin among the states that have "largely refrained from targeting transgender adults" while also not "taking extraordinary steps to protect" them — a comparatively low-risk state posture inside a federation whose overall rating for trans visitors fell after the 2025 federal rollbacks of identity documents and passport policy.

No Wisconsin-specific facility or care ban appears in the assessment's grading. The national equality-map project cataloguing state bathroom bans was cited by the research pass but its page could not be reloaded at fetch time, so it stands as a data source only.

sources.claim: July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places this state in its 'Low-Risk States' group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC) - states that have 'largely refrained from targeting transgender adults' while not taking 'extraordinary steps to protect' them.

NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (only the equality-map site's navigation shell was retrieved); the underlying MAP Equality Map page tracks state-by-state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

sources.title: Human Rights Campaign: Wisconsin Governor Vetoes Bill Targeting Lifesaving Medical Care for Transgender Youth
sources.claim: Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers on December 6, 2023 vetoed Assembly Bill 465, legislation aimed at restricting health care for transgender youth, according to the Human Rights Campaign, which positioned the veto as keeping the care restriction from taking effect in Wisconsin. The press release quotes HRC's Wisconsin state director welcoming the decision. No gender-affirming-care ban for minors became law in Wisconsin, consistent with the record's low-risk grading of the state's posture toward transgender people.

sources.title: Wisconsin governor vetoes transgender high school athletics ban
sources.claim: Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers vetoed on April 2, 2024 a bill passed by the Republican-controlled Legislature that would have limited high school athletes to teams matching the gender they were assigned at birth; the bill's sponsor called the veto 'disgusting'. AP reports Evers had promised the veto since the bill was introduced and that Democrats did not have enough votes to stop its passage in the Legislature. The veto documents Wisconsin declining to enact the trans-athlete ban, and the story records no public-facility or adult-care restriction.

sources.title: UW Health, Children's Wisconsin pause gender-affirming care for minors after HHS directive
sources.claim: UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced on January 13, 2026 that they would pause gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18, after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors; WMTV reports Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul had joined a coalition of states to block the HHS declaration. Mental and behavioural health services continued. The pause flows from federal funding pressure on Wisconsin hospitals rather than any state ban.

sources.title: Transgender bill hearings in Wisconsin: What you need to know
sources.claim: Wisconsin Watch reports that October 2023 public hearings in the Wisconsin Legislature on bills to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including the 'Help Not Harm Act' based on model legislation, and to restrict transgender sports participation were marked by misinformation, with lawmaker questions indicating gaps in basic knowledge. The WIAA and NCAA retained their own policies addressing transgender athletes. The piece documents the legislative push against transgender rights in Wisconsin and the absence of enacted bans at the time.

records.name: Michigan
records.current_summary:
An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment credits Michigan with "fairly robust non-discrimination policies" and places it in its low-risk band, while noting the state falls short in healthcare equity and in protections for incarcerated transgender people.

The 2025 federal document and passport rollbacks apply to visitors here as in every state. Regional context from the research pass: a federal judge declined to halt a neighbouring state's gender-care ban for minors — courts have let such bans stand — but that case is not Michigan-specific evidence.

sources.claim: Anti-trans legal risk assessment map, July 2026 update: places Michigan in the 'Low-Risk States' tier and specifically notes that Michigan (with Nevada) has 'enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies but fall short in ensuring healthcare equity and providing protections for incarcerated transgender individuals'; the map also designates the United States 'Do Not Travel' for transgender people overall and grades Wisconsin 'largely refrained from targeting' adults without specialising in protection.

NOTE: this national-broadcaster article is about a neighbouring state — a federal judge denied civil-rights advocates' request to halt that state's ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors (hormones/puberty blockers barred after 28 August, transition surgeries for minors prohibited, the law sunsets in 2027); included as context for how courts have responded to regional care bans, not Michigan-specific evidence.

sources.title: LGBTQIA+ rights in Michigan - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's LGBTQIA+ rights in Michigan page records that on 8 March 2023 Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed the first major expansion of the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, codifying sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections into state law, with such discrimination already unlawful since a July 2022 Michigan Supreme Court ruling. The legislature also banned conversion therapy (2023) and the gay/trans panic defense (2024), and a March 2025 House resolution urged the state high-school athletic association to exclude transgender athletes from girls' sports. Directly supports the record's 'fairly robust non-discrimination policies' characterization.

sources.title: Michigan House advises MHSAA to ban transgender athletes from girls' sports - Upper Michigan's Source
sources.claim: Upper Michigan's Source (13 March 2025, by Stephen DeLadurantaye) reported from Lansing that the Michigan House passed a non-binding resolution urging the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) to ban transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. The measure is advisory only and does not change state law or the state's non-discrimination protections.

records.name: Nevada
records.current_summary:
An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment places Nevada in its low-risk band — directly below the most-protective group — crediting "fairly robust non-discrimination policies" while noting the state falls short in healthcare equity and in protections for incarcerated transgender people.

The 2025 federal document and passport rollbacks apply here as across the federation. The national equality-map tracker of facility bans was cited by the research pass but could not be reloaded at fetch time, and stands as a data source only.

sources.claim: July 2026 assessment credits Nevada with 'fairly robust non-discrimination policies' but says it falls short on healthcare equity and protections for incarcerated transgender people; listed in the Low-Risk group (AZ, DE, ME, MI, NV, PA, VA, WI, DC), directly below the most-protective tier.

NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (only the equality-map site's navigation shell was retrieved); the underlying MAP Equality Map page tracks state-by-state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nevada - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's state page for Nevada records that the state's anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, and that since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required and similar changes available for driver's licenses and state IDs; a May 2017 law (signed June 22, 2017) abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. In March 2018 the state's Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery costs, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and Nevada offers an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licenses, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required (2019). In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the legislature-passed 2023 omnibus bill SB 302 shielding gender-affirming care and abortion was vetoed by the governor; a separate June 2023 bill requiring health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments became law effective January 1, 2024. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States - Wikipedia
sources.claim: The national-framework page that governs federal policy applying within Nevada: on January 20, 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14168 ('Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government'), redefining federal policy to recognise only two sexes based on gametes, revoking federal recognition of a third gender and directing agencies to implement the binary definition; on January 22, 2025 the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes, ending the 'X' passport option available on a self-identification basis from 2022 to 2025, while passports issued before January 2025 with markers not matching assigned sex remain valid. The page also records the June 18, 2025 US Supreme Court ruling in United States v. Skrmetti holding state bans on gender-affirming care for minors constitutional. This confirms the 2025 federal document and passport rollbacks the record says apply here as across the federation.

records.name: Maryland
records.current_summary:
Maryland is one of the most legally protective states in the country: its Trans Health Equity Act took effect 1 January 2024 and mandates Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment — hormones, puberty blockers and surgery — for an estimated 94,000 trans residents, a coverage layer the July 2026 national risk map counts among the country's most protective.

Protective law has not produced safety. An overlay of Trans Murder Monitoring records (428+ confirmed US killings 2008–2025, a conservative undercount) puts Maryland at 11.1 killings per 100,000 trans women per year, the second-highest state rate, and in 2026 two Black trans women were shot dead in Baltimore ten weeks apart — the most recent, Sophie Lee, 27, killed in Charles Village with the suspect at large. Visitors should weigh the protections against that violence data.
records.current_localsOnly: The Trans Health Equity Act's Medicaid expansion covers gender-affirming treatment for the state's estimated 94,000 trans and nonbinary residents - a care-access benefit a short-term visitor does not draw on.

sources.claim: July 2026 analysis plots recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score: Maryland sits in the 'Safest States' band (law score 23.5) with 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana tops both worst-laws (24.7) and recorded (11.6) - the piece's point is that protective law floors do not by themselves predict incident counts.

Report of September 13, 2026: on Friday September 11, 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman (Sophie Lee) was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died - the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Firm-blog tracker with May 2024 updates on Maryland's Trans Health Equity Act: the Act passed the Maryland House of Delegates (page dated May 20, 2024, sponsor line Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery), extending Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment; page follows the measure's path through the Maryland Senate.

records.name: Colorado
records.current_summary:
Colorado's anti-discrimination law (CADA) expressly covers gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing and public accommodation — the last directly traveler-relevant for hotels, restaurants and venues — and 2025 legislative materials record the state's gender-related protections being expanded again that year. A July 2026 national risk map lists Colorado among the country's Most Protective states, citing insurance-coverage mandates and refuge protections for people fleeing restrictive states.

Federal 2025 document and passport restrictions still apply here as across the federation.
records.current_localsOnly: Employment and housing protections under CADA are resident-facing; the public-accommodation coverage is the part a visitor directly uses.

sources.claim: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (403); the underlying source is the Colorado Legislature's 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation (r25-595), documenting that CADA's non-discrimination coverage — employment, housing and public accommodations, expressly including gender identity and gender expression — was expanded again in 2025.

July 2026 assessment lists Colorado among 'Most Protective States (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ...)'; the page also counts Colorado among states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage, and among the top states for trans people seeking security.

sources.title: Colorado Supreme Court sides with transgender youth in fight against Children's Hospital Colorado
sources.claim: The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on May 18, 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated the state's anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume the care (puberty blockers, hormone therapy). Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity'; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system. The ruling documents Colorado's highest court actively enforcing the gender-identity protections on which this record's anti-discrimination claim rests.

sources.title: Colorado voters will decide whether to ban trans kids from gendered sports, outlaw gender-affirming surgery for children
sources.claim: Colorado voters will decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender kids from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified the voter signatures on the three measures including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking (The Colorado Sun, Mar. 17, 2026). The initiatives were pushed by conservative activists and would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state law. They are the first statewide ballot-level counter-pressure to Colorado's protective legal posture that this record documents.

sources.title: Colorado to suspend Medicaid coverage for some gender-affirming care for youth due to new federal rule
sources.claim: Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning Oct. 13, 2026, because a new federal rule finalized in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child program); the state's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage 'will require legislative action' (The Colorado Sun, Aug. 21, 2026). About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, and patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period while behavioural healthcare is unaffected. The suspension shows Colorado's protections operating under direct federal-funding pressure, relevant to a trans visitor's assessment of the state.

records.name: Minnesota
records.current_summary: Went furthest on non-cooperation: HF 146 (2023) declares out-of-state anti-trans law “against the public policy of this state” and blocks out-of-state warrants, arrests and extradition related to gender-affirming care — a state refusing to enforce other states' hostility. Most Protective tier; among the safest legal environments for a trans visitor in the US. Clearly above the national score 0.36.
records.current_localsOnly: HF 146's shields — subpoena, warrant and extradition bars around gender-affirming care — operate on residents, providers and families; visitors mainly read them as official posture.

sources.claim: Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146): gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act 'is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied' in pending cases; the law amends provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions related to out-of-state laws on gender-affirming health care.
July 2026 assessment lists Minnesota among 'Most Protective States (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ...)', the tier the piece treats as strongest.

records.name: New Jersey
records.current_summary: The safest measured jurisdiction in the country: lowest per-capita killing rate in the state-by-state dataset (3.4 per 100k trans women/yr; 4 recorded deaths 2008–2025) — half the general US homicide rate — inside the Most Protective legal tier. Clearly above the national score 0.36.

sources.claim: State-by-state dataset of killings of trans women 2008-2025 (TGEU Trans Murder Monitoring / Williams Institute): New Jersey = 3.4 per 100k per year (4 recorded deaths), labelled 'Safest States', against 428 US trans women confirmed killed since 2008. Central finding: state anti-trans law hostility does not correlate with where trans women are killed (trendline nearly flat over the 26-state comparison) - law predicts government treatment (ID, healthcare, bathroom access), not private violence.

July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills (youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate/driver-license restrictions, end of legal recognition): New Jersey sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier (CA, CO, CT, HI, IL, MA, MD, MN, NJ, NM, NY, OR, RI, VT, WA), whose laws have 'gone above and beyond in safeguarding' trans rights. Contrast tier: worst-law states carry up to 5-year prison terms (Idaho) or arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use (Florida).
